Loss and transitions

Does grief have stages?

The five stages are a popular but inaccurate idea. Most people cope with loss better than they expect.

Denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The five stages of grief are so well known that many people believe they must go through them in order, and worry if they do not.

Where the stages come from

They were proposed by the psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross in 1969, based on interviews with people who were dying, not with bereaved people. Her book was very valuable for opening up talk about death, but the stages were not based on systematic research and were not meant to be a fixed sequence.

What studies show

In 2007, Paul Maciejewski and colleagues followed people who had lost a relative. The most frequent emotion was not anger or denial but yearning, and acceptance was present from the start. The emotions did not follow an order: they came and went.

The psychologist George Bonanno has shown that the most common reaction to loss is resilience: many people feel intense pain but keep functioning, and their distress eases within months. That does not mean they loved the person who died any less.

When grief gets complicated

In a minority, the pain is still intense and paralysing after a year, with constant yearning, difficulty accepting the death and a sense that life has lost its meaning. This is prolonged grief disorder, and it can be treated.

Staying connected

For much of the twentieth century it was thought that getting over grief required "letting go" of the person who had died. In 1996, Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman proposed the idea of continuing bonds: many people keep a relationship with the person who has died, talking to them, remembering their advice or keeping objects, and this is not a sign of pathological grief. What matters is not cutting the tie but transforming it so it can coexist with the life that goes on.

Moving between loss and life

Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described the dual process model. A grieving person moves back and forth between two tasks: facing the loss (crying, remembering, missing) and facing the changes it brings (new tasks, new routines, new roles). Both are necessary, and taking breaks from the pain, distracting yourself or even laughing is not denying the loss but part of the healthy way of working through it.

What usually helps

  • Do not force an order or compare yourself with what you "should" feel.
  • Talk about the person, remember them and keep rituals.
  • Accept practical help from those around you.
  • Look after the basics: sleeping, eating and moving.
If after a long time the pain stops you living your life, or you have thoughts of not wanting to live, seek help. In Spain you can call 024.

References

  1. Maciejewski, P. K. et al. (2007). An empirical examination of the stage theory of grief. JAMA, 297(7), 716–723.
  2. Bonanno, G. A. (2004). Loss, trauma, and human resilience. American Psychologist, 59(1), 20–28.
  3. Klass, D., Silverman, P. R. y Nickman, S. L. (Eds.) (1996). Continuing Bonds: New Understandings of Grief. Washington: Taylor & Francis.
  4. Stroebe, M. y Schut, H. (1999). The dual process model of coping with bereavement: rationale and description. Death Studies, 23(3), 197–224.
